reasoning.Student A:
My goal is to maximize my utility, which is the value I get from the school I am matched to. I also want to avoid being unmatched. My values for the schools are w = $56, x = $64, y = $58, z = $46. My priorities are w: 1, x: 2, y: 1, z: 2.

Since I have top priority at both w and y, I am almost guaranteed to get into my top choice between these two. Since y > w in value, I should rank y higher than w.

Now, I must consider x and z. I have second priority at x and z. Since x > z, I would prefer to attend x than z.
If I rank x before w and y, and I don't get x, I will be rejected and I will propose to y, which I have top priority at.
If I rank x last, I might end up with z, which is worse than w and y.
If I rank x second, after y, I will get y if I don't get x. If I rank x second after w, I will get w if I don't get x. Since x > y > w > z, I should rank x second.
If I rank x third, I will get w or y before I get x, which is not optimal.

Therefore, I should rank the schools in the order y > x > w > z.

Let's consider some alternative rankings and why they are worse.
Ranking x > y > w > z: If I don't get x, I will get y. However, if many people also rank y highly, I might be rejected from y. In that case, I will get w.
Ranking w > y > x > z: I will get w for sure, since I have top priority. But y > w, so this is not optimal.
Ranking y > w > x > z: I will get y for sure, since I have top priority. But x > w, so I might prefer x.
Ranking y > w > z > x: This is bad since x > z.

If I don't get x, I will be matched to y, w, or z. In situations where x is available, then x > y > w > z is better than y > x > w > z. In situations where x is not available, then the two rankings are equivalent. Thus, x > y > w > z dominates y > x > w > z.

I will stick with x > y > w > z.
